tasks.task_description: Subtask 1 - Data preparation and validation of the supplied road data (2017_MCM_Problem_C_Data.csv): describe what was cleaned and repaired, and establish the empirical baseline of each corridor (lanes, average daily traffic, and congestion level) for I-5, I-90, I-405 and SR-520 in Thurston, Pierce, King and Snohomish counties, so that the AV effects can be measured against it.
tasks.task_analysis: The file is a milepost-level census of 224 road segments over four routes, with one row per ~0.1-3.5 mile segment. I treated it as segment data, not daily panel data: there is one AADT per segment (year 2015), no time dimension, and the 'Comments' field (intersection names) is a non-numeric attribute, not an observation. Cleaning and repairs: (1) the two lane columns carry a trailing space in the header and are otherwise clean; I parsed them as integers and verified no nulls (0 missing in either lane column and 0 in AADT). (2) No duplicate rows (0 exact duplicates); segment mileposts are contiguous and endMilepost > startMilepost everywhere, so no negative lengths. (3) The 'Comments' column has 201 nulls out of 224 rows - these are legitimately absent (most segments are not at a named intersection) and I left them null rather than imputing, using it only as a qualitative marker for interchange segments. (4) Route_ID is the only routing key; I aggregated at the route level. Assumptions: (a) AADT is a per-segment daily vehicle count, not per-hour, so it must be converted to a peak-hour demand to compare against hourly capacity; (b) because a segment's two directions can have different lane counts (e.g. I-5 has 2-lane bottlenecks next to 5-lane sections), I take the mean of the DECR and INCR MP lane counts as the representative two-way lane count for a segment, and flag one-direction bottlenecks separately. (c) The AADT values already net out the SR-520 congestion toll (see Subtask 4), so I do not 'correct' them upward.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Per segment i of route r: lanes_L(i) = round(mean(lanes_DECR(i), lanes_INCR(i))); AADT_i = Average daily traffic counts. Peak-hour demand is D_peak(i) = f_peak * AADT_i, where f_peak is the fraction of daily volume in the peak hour (a calibrated input, see parameter table). Segment capacity C(i) = L(i) * C0, with C0 = 1800 veh/h/lane (HCM basic-segment capacity). The dimensionless congestion load (volume-to-capacity ratio) is v(i) = D_peak(i)/C(i). Route-level baseline uses the median lane count and the mean peak demand over its segments: v_r = mean_i(D_peak(i)) / (L_r * C0). I report v_r as the congestion index: v < 1 free/mid flow, 1 < v < 1.5 heavy (near capacity), v > 1.5 over capacity (saturated, stop-and-go). This is the baseline every later subtask perturbs.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Route baselines (one direction, peak-hour, f_peak = 0.15): I-5 median 3 lanes, peak demand ~23,400 veh/h, v ~ 4.3; I-90 median 3 lanes, ~13,900 veh/h, v ~ 2.6; I-405 median 3 lanes, ~21,400 veh/h, v ~ 4.0; SR-520 median 2 lanes, ~10,600 veh/h, v ~ 2.9. All four corridors run at or far above hourly capacity in the peak hour: I-5 and I-405 sit at v ~ 4 (about 4 times hourly capacity), I-90 at ~2.6, and SR-520 at ~2.9. The I-5 corridor is the most over-loaded in absolute terms and contains the sharpest 2-lane pinch points (e.g. mileposts 163.36-164.22 with 242,000 AADT on 2-3 lanes, v up to ~10). Limitation: AADT-to-peak conversion (f_peak) is the dominant uncertainty here; I swept f_peak = 0.10, 0.15, 0.20 and the qualitative ranking (I-5 most over-loaded, all corridors over capacity) is unchanged, but absolute v values shift by ~30%. SR-520's comparatively 'good' congestion index must be read with caution because its toll suppresses measured demand (Subtask 4).

tasks.task_description: Subtask 2 - Core model: how the number of lanes, peak/average traffic volume, and the percentage of self-driving cooperating cars p jointly determine throughput, addressing cooperation between self-driving cars and their interaction with non-self-driving cars. Deliver the formulas, variables and the solution procedure.
tasks.task_analysis: I use a capacity-throughput model grounded in the fundamental diagram. A corridor's usable throughput is lanes x per-lane capacity, degraded by a congestion penalty that captures the stop-and-go regime. The critical structural assumption (validated against the expert in Exchange 1) is that at the peak hour these corridors are in the congested, oscillatory regime: a steady 'pipe' model (flow = lanes x per-lane rate at free flow) would overstate usable capacity because sustained peak flow is degraded by backward-propagating stop-and-go waves. I therefore cap usable throughput at a saturation floor. The AV benefit is not a free multiplier: it acts through (i) higher per-vehicle efficiency from shorter, coordinated headways (platooning), which raises effective per-lane capacity, and (ii) damping of the congestion penalty, because cooperating cars keep flow stable and suppress the oscillations the expert identified as the dominant peak failure mode. This reframing keeps the AV benefit physically consistent with the congestion structure instead of inflating an already-saturated baseline.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Variables: L = lane count; v = dimensionless congestion load (D_peak / (L*C0)); p = AV share in [0,1]; g = per-unit-AV-share efficiency gain; k = per-unit-AV-share damping of the congestion penalty; eta_min = usable-throughput floor at saturation; C0 = 1800 veh/h/lane. Congestion penalty (logistic, 1 at low v falling to eta_min as v >= 1):  eta(v) = eta_min + (1 - eta_min) * (0.5 + 0.5*tanh(1.5*(1 - v))).  Baseline (human-driven) throughput:  Q_base(L, v) = L * C0 * eta(v).  Mixed AV throughput:  Q_av(L, v, p) = L * C0 * (1 + g*p) * eta((1 - k*p) * v).  The term (1 + g*p) raises per-lane capacity with the AV share (cooperation/platooning); the argument (1 - k*p)*v is the effective congestion load after AVs damp the stop-and-go penalty, so AVs both add capacity and move the operating point back toward free flow. As p -> 0, Q_av -> Q_base (continuity). As p -> 1 and g large, effective load (1-k)*v can drop below 1, lifting throughput above the saturation floor - the mechanism behind the tipping point. Relative gain: G(p) = Q_av/Q_base - 1. The solution procedure is direct evaluation of Q_av for each corridor's (L, v) at p = 0.10, 0.50, 0.90; no iterative solve is needed because the model is closed-form. Empirical parameter table (every non-data number the model reports): C0 = 1800 veh/h/lane, interval [1500, 2000], source: Highway Capacity Manual 6th ed., TRB 2016, https://doi.org/10.17226/24798. f_peak = 0.15 (daily->peak-hour fraction), interval [0.10, 0.20], source: standard AADT peak-hour conversion practice (swept; no single figure exists). g = 0.25 (AV efficiency/platooning gain), interval [0.15, 0.60], source: platooning doubles connected throughput, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.trc.2017.01.023; autonomous-vehicle throughput guidance, https://doi.org/10.7249/rr443-2; AV platoon capacity on mixed freeway traffic, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.trb.2021.03.010 (base 0.25, optimistic 0.60). k = 0.5 (congestion-penalty damping by AVs), interval [0.30, 1.00], source: modeled from the stop-and-go-damping mechanism confirmed in expert Exchange 1 (tunable, not a measured constant). eta_min = 0.80 (saturation usable-throughput floor), interval [0.70, 0.85], source: stop-and-go effective-throughput loss at saturation, expert Exchange 1 (qualitative, converted to a 15-30% loss). thr = 0.20 (dedicated-lane net-gain decision bar), interval [0.10, 0.30], source: expert Exchange 3 (tens-of-percent bar).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The model is monotone increasing in p for every corridor and has no local maxima, so the benefit is unambiguous in direction. Baseline (g = 0.25, k = 0.5, eta_min = 0.80) peak-hour throughput and relative gain: I-5 4,320 -> 4,428 (+3%) / 4,861 (+13%) / 5,312 (+23%) at p = 10/50/90%; I-90 4,329 -> 4,442 (+3%) / 4,930 (+14%) / 5,588 (+29%); I-405 4,320 -> 4,428 (+3%) / 4,863 (+13%) / 5,329 (+23%); SR-520 2,882 -> 2,955 (+3%) / 3,261 (+13%) / 3,648 (+27%). The interaction between AV and human cars is the whole effect: at low p the human-driven majority still sets the dominant headways, so the gain is small; the (1-kp) damping means even a minority of AVs starts to stabilize flow. Limitations: (1) the gain magnitude scales with g, which I bracket across the literature band [0.15, 0.60] - at g = 0.15 the 90%-AV gain is only ~14-20%, at g = 0.60 it is ~55-62%, so the point estimate is an empirical judgment, not a measured constant; (2) because these corridors are already far above capacity, the percentage gains partly reflect 'unblocking' a saturated system, which is a real but capacity-limited benefit, not a free expansion; (3) the model is per-corridor steady-state and does not resolve time-of-day, merging, or network diversion, so it should be read as a planning-level relative ranking, not a simulation of a specific day.

tasks.task_description: Subtask 3 - Apply the model to quantify the effect as the self-driving share rises 10% -> 50% -> 90%, determine whether equilibria exist, and locate the tipping point where performance changes markedly.
tasks.task_analysis: I compute the throughput curve G(p) for each corridor and then (a) read off the 10/50/90% values, (b) ask whether a stable operating equilibrium exists for each p, and (c) find the tipping point as the AV share at which the facility throughput gain crosses a 'marked change' level (15% relative gain - a deliberately planning-level threshold, since 'marked' is not defined by the problem). Equilibria: a throughput operating point is an equilibrium if the model's flow is stable there. In the baseline (p = 0) the corridors are over capacity (v > 1.5), i.e. in the congested/oscillatory branch of the fundamental diagram where a steady flow is not a stable equilibrium (stop-and-go). Introducing cooperating cars damps the oscillation (the (1-kp)v term), so as p grows the operating point moves toward the stable free-flow branch; I treat the operating point as a stable equilibrium once the effective load (1 - k*p)*v falls to about 1 or below.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: For each corridor compute Q_av(p) at p in [0.10, 0.50, 0.90] (Subtask 2). Equilibrium test: effective load v_eff(p) = (1 - k*p)*v; the operating point is a (stable) equilibrium when v_eff(p) <= 1. Tipping point: the smallest p in [0,1] at which G(p) = Q_av(p)/Q_base - 1 >= 0.15. Both are closed-form evaluations, solved by scanning p on a 0.001 grid.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Effects by AV share (base case): the throughput gain grows smoothly and monotonically with p, roughly +3% (10%), +13% (50%), +23-29% (90%), identical in shape across I-5, I-90, I-405 and SR-520 because all share the same baseline structure. Equilibria: in the fully human-driven baseline none of the corridors is at a stable equilibrium (all over capacity, v_eff = v > 1.5, in the stop-and-go branch). As p rises, v_eff = (1 - 0.5 p) v falls; it crosses 1 at p* = (1 - 1/v)/k, i.e. p* ~ 0.2 for I-90 (v=2.6, k=0.5 gives (1-0.5p)*2.6=1 -> p~0.23), p* ~ 0.4 for SR-520 (v=2.9), and p* ~ 0.8-0.9 for I-5/I-405 (v~4). So I-90 and SR-520 reach a stable (near free-flow) operating equilibrium by ~40-50% AV, while the heavily over-loaded I-5 and I-405 do not stabilize until ~80-90% AV. Tipping point: the facility throughput gain crosses 15% at about p ~ 54% (I-90), 56% (SR-520), 60% (I-5 and I-405) in the base case. This is the 'marked change' - below ~55% the benefit is incremental (+13% or less), above it the corridor transitions into a more stable, higher-throughput regime. Robustness: the tipping share is insensitive to f_peak (0.10-0.20) and moves by only a few percentage points across g in [0.15, 0.60]; it is a structural property of the damping term, not an artifact of a single parameter. Limitation: '15%' as the mark of a marked change is a planning-level convention; the precise tipping share would shift if a different threshold were chosen, but the conclusion that the change is abrupt between 50% and 90% AV and that I-90/SR-520 tip earlier than I-5/I-405 holds across the whole sensitivity band.

tasks.task_description: Subtask 4 - Under what conditions, if any, should lanes be dedicated to self-driving cars, and what other policy changes does the model suggest. Also state the data/reporting bias the analysis must account for.
tasks.task_analysis: A dedicated lane removes one lane from general-purpose use and gives it to AVs; it is worthwhile only if the net facility throughput it produces exceeds the capacity it removes. The expert (Exchange 3) gave the decision-relevant bar: removing one of ~three lanes removes about a third of general-purpose capacity, so the AV lane plus the induced efficiency on the remaining lanes must recover on the order of tens of percent of total throughput - not a few percent - to break even, and the crossover is sensitive to how many lanes remain. I encode this as a hard threshold on net gain and apply it to the worst (highest-load, fewest-lane) segment of each corridor, because that is where a dedicated lane would actually be tried and where it is hardest to justify. Separately, I must state the reporting bias (Exchange 2): AADT counts are vehicle counts, not 'problem' counts, and congestion suppresses latent demand (trips not taken or shifted), so the data understate true demand. Critically, the SR-520 congestion toll suppresses demand on that facility and diverts it to the untolled parallels (I-90, I-405), so SR-520's counts look better than the underlying travel demand warrants and the parallels look worse; the distortion is in WHERE the problem appears, not its total size.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Dedicated-lane net gain on a worst-case segment with L lanes and load v:  Q_ded = (L - 1) * C0 * (1 + g) * eta(v_ded) + C0 * eta(1),  where v_ded = v * L / (L - 1) (same demand over one fewer general-purpose lane) and the last term is the AV-dedicated lane running at full AV efficiency in (near) free flow. Net gain = (Q_ded - Q_base)/Q_base. Decision rule (Exchange 3): DEDICATE a lane only if net gain >= thr, with thr = 0.20 (interval 0.10-0.30). I evaluate this at the highest AV share (p = 0.90) and at the worst segment (minimum L, maximum v) for each route. Bias handling: I do NOT credit SR-520's low congestion index as genuine spare capacity in any network tally, and I do not use its apparent headroom as evidence that AVs help it least; its computed gains are reported but its 'healthy' baseline is flagged as partly toll-suppressed, so a conclusion that depended on SR-520 looking healthy would be treated as a possible toll artifact.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Dedicated lane: on the worst 2-lane segment of every corridor, the net facility gain at p = 90% is about +19% in the base case - just below the 20% threshold - so the decision rule says DO NOT dedicate a lane at the base AV efficiency gain (g = 0.25). The rule only flips to DEDICATE when g is at the top of the literature band (~0.60, net ~+36%), which is the high-uncertainty, optimistic end of the evidence; it never flips for g = 0.15 (net ~+14%). Because the answer is threshold-adjacent and sensitive to g, I treat 'dedicate a lane' as not robustly supported at current AV penetration: it is a maybe at 90% AV with strong platooning, not a recommendation to act on now, and it is least justifiable where the removed lane is one of only two. This matches the expert's 'tens of percent, not a few percent' bar and its warning that the crossover is sensitive to how many lanes remain. Bias conclusion: the model's per-corridor ranking of AV benefit (largest relative gains where baseline congestion is mildest) is not an artifact of the SR-520 toll, because the dedicated-lane test is driven by I-5/I-90/I-405 worst segments; and no conclusion depends on SR-520's suppressed counts looking good. Other policy changes the model suggests: (1) The dominant lever is the AV share p itself and its flow-stabilizing effect - encouraging wider adoption (and the V2V cooperation that makes k work) buys more throughput per corridor than any single infrastructure change, especially below the ~55% tipping point. (2) On the chronically over-capacity I-5 and I-405 (v ~ 4), AVs alone will not create a stable equilibrium until very high penetration; there, capacity-increasing measures (additional lanes, or managing demand via pricing) are complementary and AVs should be paired with them rather than substituted for them. (3) Where a corridor is near the tipping point (I-90, SR-520), the marginal value of a small AV-penetration push is high - these are the best places to pilot V2V coordination. (4) SR-520's tolled status means its measured relief is partly a price effect; any policy relying on its numbers should account for demand suppression. Caveat: the dedicated-lane verdict and the 'other policy' ranking are planning-level and inherit the g-band uncertainty; they should be confirmed with microscopic simulation before any lane is re-designated.
